idiom_name: static slot array with linear probing and an occupancy flag
implementation_notes: C has no map, so the memo is a hand-written table: an array of (key, value, used) slots plus a hash over the argument tuple and a probe sequence. Size it for the key domain you actually have and leave headroom - the hsearch(3) page notes that hash tables perform better when the table holds at least about 25% free space - and keep an explicit occupied flag, because a sentinel value cannot distinguish an empty slot from a legitimately computed result. The classic structure is replaced by the table plus a guarded lookup at the top of the function; when the domain is genuinely small and dense (an index, a small enum) the classic form is still justified as a plain array indexed by the key, with a separate bitmap for occupancy and no hashing at all.
pitfalls: A sentinel such as 0 or -1 cannot mark an empty slot if the function can legitimately return it; keep a separate occupancy flag or bitmap.
The load factor is not managed for you: a nearly full table degrades to linear scans (and hsearch(3) returns ENOMEM when it is full).
Nothing in C makes the table thread-safe: a shared memo needs a mutex around the probe, and a memoized function that recurses through the same table must not hold that mutex.
There is no eviction: a table sized for a bounded domain releases nothing, so a growing domain must either be reset explicitly or bounded by construction.

variants.name: POSIX hsearch table (one process-global, string keys)
variants.implementation_notes: POSIX supplies a single process-global hash table with string keys: hcreate() fixes the maximum number of entries up front (it cannot be changed later), hsearch() with ENTER inserts on a miss and returns the existing entry on a hit, and the caller formats the key from the arguments into a stable string. That saves writing the table itself, which is exactly the case it is still justified for - one small string-keyed memo in a single-threaded tool - at the price of a global resource: only one such table can exist at a time, entries can be added but not deleted, the key is the string itself, and the glibc page marks hcreate/hsearch/hdestroy as MT-Unsafe race:hsearch, so the GNU hcreate_r/hsearch_r reentrant variants or a second hand-rolled table are needed for anything else.
pitfalls: hcreate() fixes the maximum entry count permanently; filling the table makes further ENTER calls fail with ENOMEM, and the man page recommends sizing at least 25% above the expected maximum.
Only one hash table exists per process: a second memo needs the GNU hcreate_r/hsearch_r variants or its own table.
Entries cannot be deleted, and hdestroy() does not free the buffers your key/data pointers point at, so the caller owns that bookkeeping.
The table is unsynchronised (MT-Unsafe race:hsearch): concurrent use needs an external mutex, and the keys must stay valid for the table's lifetime.
